newsitem.title: USA: Clinton holds to veto threat on nuclear waste bill.
newsitem.headline: Clinton holds to veto threat on nuclear waste bill.

text.p: The Clinton administration Thursday vowed again to veto a bill that would force the Energy Department to build a temporary storage site in Nevada for spent fuel from nuclear power plants.

Under Secretary of Energy Thomas Grumbly repeated the Clinton administration's objections that the bill, which was backed last year by 63 senators and reintroduced this year, would effectively halt plans for a permanent dump for the highly radioactive waste collecting at commercial reactors.
"If S.104 were presented to the president in its current form, the president would veto the bill," he said.

Under a 1982 law, reinforced by a court decision last July, the government was supposed to start taking over utilities' nuclear waste by the end of January 1998. But the Energy Department does not expect to have a dump ready until 2010 at the earliest.
The 1982 law required utilities to pay about $600 million a year into a nuclear waste fund for building a graveyard.

In face of the long delays, utilities have been pressing for an interim facility to relieve them from storing the waste, and 33 of them sued the government last week to freeze $600 million in the fund until a temporary dump is built.

"It is unsafe to let this dangerous radioactive material continue to accumulate at more than 80 sites all across the country," Senator Frank Murkowski, an Alaska Republican, said at a hearing of the Senate Energy Committee, which he chairs.
However, an independent review board and the Nuclear Regulatory Commission have said storing the spent fuel on site at nuclear plants is safe.

"There are no compelling technical or safety reasons to move spent fuel to a centralized storage facility for the next few years," Jared Conlon, chairman of the Nuclear Waste Technical Review board, said in testimony for the committee.
Grumbly objected to provisions in the Senate bill that would limit the amount of time the administration had to identify potential sites for a temporary facility.

The bill calls for the administration to make a decision on temporary storage in Nevada when the Energy Department determines whether Nevada's Yucca Mountain is viable for a permanent dump, which the department plans to decide in 1998.

However, if Yucca Mountain proves to be unsuitable, the bill gives the government just 18 months to choose another site for temporary storage. "We need more like three and half to four years," Grumbly said.

But he repeated Wednesday that so far there were "no showstoppers" to developing Yucca Mountain, but the administration did not want to divert resources from its underground studies in order to build a temporary facility.
Nevada is deeply opposed to storing nuclear waste in the state and fears that an aboveground temporary facility would automatically become a permanent dump.
The Senator Richard Bryan, a Nevada Democrat, said if Clinton vetoed the bill, "I expect we will have the votes in the Senate to sustain the president's veto."
The committee is expected to vote on the bill soon.
